SAFE, INCLUSIVE COMMUNITY
GOAL
Our community is safe and inclusive. Our first responders are
well-equipped and staffed by a team of people who take a
community service approach to their work, resulting in lower
crime rates and faster response times. The community
appreciates and supports their work.
PROGRESS UPDATES 2024-2025
The Fire Department has replaced eight (8) emergency response vehicles in three (3)
years for a combined cost of nearly $5,000,000.
Police Department staffing levels have increased, including a new social worker &
school resource officer. Technology improvements include increased ShotSpotter &
camera coverage.
Added 25 Flock LPR Cameras, One LVT Surveillance Camera, in process of
incorporating 20 additional body worn cameras, one Skydio Drone and a mobile
command trailer.
KEY STRATEGIES
Maintain police force census and implement proven strategies for reducing crime, including a 3-
pronged staffing approach that includes community service officers, law enforcement, and social
workers to reduce crime.
Reduce fire department turnover through a focus on local recruitment.
Increase fire department staffing to deploy a third (3rd) full-time ambulance.
The fire department continues to invest in technology and efficiencies.
FD capital projects completed; new station generator at Central Station, new VHF radio network
replacement, replacement of concrete drives at station 1 and Central.
Deploy more technology to reduce gun violence & improve the efficiency of the police force. Increase
lighting, camera locations & drone use in high-crime areas.
Support active Neighborhood Watch programs.
Retain a diverse team (police, fire, and throughout City staff) to reflect the community we serve.
Plan for a downtown public safety facility to replace the police station and the Adams St. fire station.
Streamline emergency communications to improve service & create efficiencies.
TARGETS & MILESTONES
Police force census & demographics
Fire department census & demographics
FD improve upon ISO (Insurance Services
Organization) rating from class 3 to class 2.
Maintain or improve upon annual response times of
4 < minutes.

Staff census & demographics
Technology deployments
Crime rates & incidents
2026-2028 Strategic Framework 03

NEIGHBORHOODS & HOUSING
GOAL
Freeport’s neighborhoods are safe and affordable with a
small-town feel that attracts families and a growing
workforce. Our neighborhoods are connected to the many
parks, recreation areas, shopping, and schools. Residents
have ownership of their neighborhoods and take pride in
them.
PROGRESS UPDATES 2024-2025
Tree removal has exceeded projected numbers; 422 trees removed
Planted 150 Trees on Demolition Lots
Home demolitions & blight reduction on track; 70 structures demolished
KEY STRATEGIES
Re-Fresh Freeport Initiative: continue regular clean-up program and expand to provide guidance,
incentives, and accountability to improve overall appearance of properties and neighborhoods.
Improve rental property standards & conditions by working with landlords, renters, and housing
focused organizations.
Complete a development of downtown master plan to spur development.
Continue funding & implementation of the Demolition/Blight Reduction program.
Add a nuisance inspector to ensure homes and buildings are well kept, improving safety.
Improve neighborhoods by developing a program to activate vacant lots including mapping &
categorizing lots then acting on each lot based on categories.
Continue Tree Removal/Replacement Program including planting of new trees along with stump
removal and site remediation.
TARGETS & MILESTONES
Re-Fresh Freeport utilized by 200 first-time
participants by the end of 2027
800 registered rental properties tracked in Tolemi
$500,000 external funding secured and used for
demolition/blight reduction
150 tree removals and 150 tree plantings
All vacant lot categorized & activated
# chronic nuisance complaints
Downtown master plan complete

RELIABLE, STRONG
INFRASTRUCTURE
GOAL
Freeport’s infrastructure is reliable and supports the needs of
residents and economic growth. Our streets and walk/ride
infrastructure are well maintained, and our water and sewer systems
are industry leading & environmentally sustainable. Input from
elected officials, citizens, and usage/condition data inform decisions
about where to allocate resources.

ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT &
LAND USE (CONT.)
KEY STRATEGIES
The city and Greater Freeport Partnership (GFP) partner to drive the city’s economy through:
improved retention & growth of existing industry (GFP)
attraction of new industry and business to create jobs (GFP)
engagement with area workforce development partners to increase access to a skilled workforce
(GFP)
establish shovel-ready sites for new business development (COF)
provide support for small business, e.g. startup tools, basic biz services, business registration (GFP)
Expansion of retail & development of Meadows Shopping (build on initial $13 million investment).
Form a regular roundtable of city & economic development leaders to build readiness & support for
retaining, growing & attracting major employers, including identifying ideal sectors, e.g. healthcare,
technology, manufacturing (COF & GFP).
Infill strategy for commercial spaces & buildings – with focus on downtown.
Create a 5-year economic development plan for Albertus Airport focused on attracting private use &
investment (2026).
Complete interior buildout of terminal building.
Complete 3rd Ward flood mitigation project (2026).
Identify & engage with developers to spark & align investment.
Support festival district events to increase vibrancy & customer traffic downtown.
Develop pop-up market space on Main St. to foster entrepreneurship & entertainment downtown
Complete Karcher pocket park downtown on Stephenson St.
Create a residential/workforce housing development strategy for infill housing in city-owned lots and
for areas like Burchard Hills and others to increase available housing.
Explore a procurement program that gives higher consideration to local business.

CONNECTED, ACCESSIBLE
COMMUNITY
GOAL
Our community is easy to navigate and connected globally by high-
speed internet connections. Whether you drive a car, use Pretzel City
transit, a ride-share or taxi, ride a bike, or walk, getting around Freeport
is easy. Public transportation is widespread, frequent, and reliable.
Sidewalks, greenways, and nationally recognized bike facilities get us
where we want to go safely keeping us active and healthy.
PROGRESS UPDATES 2024-2025
Adams Ave Reconstruction
W. Stephenson Street Pavement Markings
ADA Ramps are being replaced on all Street Project corridors.
ADA Transition Plan and Evaluation
ADA Grievance Commission and Policy
KEY STRATEGIES
Increase bike lanes and bike/pedestrian pathways to major attractions, i.e., schools, downtown, parks,
shopping, Jane Addams Trail and Pecatonica Prairie Path.
Explore expansion of Pretzel City Area Transit (PCAT) services for a possible fixed route in addition to
on-demand services.
Improve accessibility throughout the city; establish a plan to complete ADA ramps.
Create bike/walk infrastructure along IDOT corridors, e.g. West St. & South St., and Galena Ave.
Seek and submit for external funding to support bike/walk infrastructure.
Pavement Marking changes or Bike path on Kiwanis.
Support the Dubuque/Rockford passenger rail committee to bring a train/commuter stop to Freeport.
Add 3 miles of bike & pedestrian pathways or on-road paths.

VIBRANT ARTS & CULTURE
EXPERIENCES
GOAL
Freeport’s art-and-culture sector offers extraordinary cultural
events, learning opportunities, and outdoor experiences for people
of all ages. Distinctive cultural districts are linked to Freeport’s
bustling commercial districts. Open spaces, bike paths, parks, and
greenways are abundant throughout the city. The river is accessible
for recreation and enjoyed by residents and visitors alike.
